# Diagnosing the BMW E90 Pre-Facelift REST Button Circuit

When you press the "REST" button in a pre-facelift BMW E90 and nothing happensâno LED illumination, no cabin heating activationâit is tempting to immediately assume a blown fuse. While fuses are certainly the first point of failure in these circuits, the diagnostic process requires isolating whether the issue lies in power delivery, control logic, or the button switch itself.

Based on standard BMW E-series wiring architectures, specifically for pre-facelift models, the heating zone and the control interface are often fed by distinct but related power sources. You mentioned fuses 15 and 67 as potential suspects. In many E90 variants, fuse 15 is a primary feed for interior lighting and comfort functions, while fuse 67 often supplies specific load modules like the rear heating or seat controls. However, relying on forum speculation without verifying the actual fuse box diagram for your specific VIN can lead to replacing parts that are perfectly fine.

The most efficient way to verify fuse integrity is a multimeter continuity test or an ohmmeter check. Locate the fuse box under the dashboard on the driver's side (often requiring removal of the trim panel) and in the engine bay. Identify fuses 15 and 67 visually, then remove them. Set your meter to resistance mode. A reading near zero indicates a good fuse; infinite resistance means it is blown. If both are intact, the fault is downstream.

If the fuses are confirmed good, the issue likely resides in the control logic or the button assembly itself. The E90 uses the Body Domain Controller (BDC) to manage these comfort functions. The BDC monitors the state of the REST button via a dedicated input pin. If the internal circuitry of the button fails to close the contact when pressed, or if the LED driver within the module has failed, the BDC will not register the command. This explains why neither the light turns on nor does the heating engage; the controller never receives the "enable" signal.

To test this without disassembling the entire dash immediately, you can attempt a back-probing technique. Locate the wiring harness connector behind the trim near the button location. Using a thin pick tool or a dedicated back-probe wire, gently pierce the contact for the control line (often labeled as the input signal) and the ground line. If you can bridge these points with a jumper wire and the heating activates while the LED lights up, the original switch mechanism is faulty. This is a common wear-and-tear failure mode where the internal spring contacts in the micro-switch degrade over years of thermal cycling inside the cabin.

Another potential pitfall is confusing the "REST" function with the "Comfort Access" or other climate zones. Ensure you are testing the correct zone. The pre-facelift architecture often separates front and rear heating circuits, so a fault in one fuse might not affect the other, but the button usually controls a specific mode that engages multiple loads simultaneously. If the system is designed to disable heating entirely when the REST mode is active (to save fuel or prevent overheating), verify your vehicle's logic settings in the iDrive menu, though this is less common on pre-facelift hardware which tends to be more direct.

If you decide to replace the button, sourcing an OEM replacement is crucial. Aftermarket switches often lack the precise resistance matching required by the BDC, leading to false readings or intermittent behavior. When swapping the part, ensure you disconnect the battery negative terminal first to prevent short circuits while working in the tight space of the E90 dash cavity.

If you are comfortable with deeper diagnostics and want to check for BDC communication errors, connecting an OBDII scanner that supports BMW-specific codes might reveal a "Short to Ground" or "Open Circuit" code associated with the comfort control module. However, given the symptoms describedâno light, no heatâthe mechanical switch failure is statistically the most probable cause after ruling out blown fuses 15 and 67.
